title: Tiotropium HandiHaler: Maintenance Bronchodilation and Device Safety
bottomLine: Tiotropium is a long-acting muscarinic antagonist used for COPD maintenance, not acute rescue. HandiHaler capsules are inhaled through the device and must never be swallowed.
recognize: Dry mouth is common; urinary retention or acute angle-closure glaucoma symptoms are important adverse cues.
Sudden bronchospasm after inhalation is abnormal and requires escalation.
priorities: Verify the exact inhaler/device and that the capsule is loaded into the inhalation device rather than swallowed.
Confirm a separate rescue plan exists for acute dyspnea.
assessMonitor: Monitor breath sounds, work of breathing, symptom control, urinary symptoms, eye pain/halos, and device technique.
interventions: Reinforce inhaler-device technique and maintenance use on schedule.
medicationSafety: Not a rescue bronchodilator.
Use caution with narrow-angle glaucoma, urinary retention, and significant renal impairment.
teaching: Do not swallow HandiHaler capsules; inhale the capsule contents using the prescribed device.
Keep the rescue inhaler available if prescribed.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and reinforce inhaler technique within policy; acute respiratory deterioration requires RN/provider/rapid escalation.
examTrap: Giving tiotropium as the first medication for an acute bronchospasm episode.
oneLinePearl: Tiotropium maintains airflow; it does not rescue it.

title: Budesonide/Formoterol: Controller Combination and Steroid Safety
bottomLine: Budesonide/formoterol combines an inhaled corticosteroid with a long-acting beta2 agonist for maintenance therapy. Safe nursing care centers correct inhaler use, oral-rinse teaching, monitoring for paradoxical bronchospasm and beta-agonist effects, and avoiding unsupervised regimen changes.
recognize: Oral thrush and dysphonia reflect local corticosteroid effects.
Tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, or hypokalemia can reflect beta2-agonist exposure.
priorities: Verify the prescribed role of the inhaler in the patient-specific asthma/COPD plan.
Assess inhaler technique and adherence before assuming treatment failure.
assessMonitor: Monitor symptom control, rescue-use frequency, oral cavity, heart rate, and paradoxical bronchospasm.
interventions: Reinforce mouth rinsing after inhaled corticosteroid exposure and proper actuation/inhalation technique.
medicationSafety: Do not independently reinterpret maintenance instructions as rescue instructions.
Avoid duplicate LABA therapy unless specifically ordered.
complications: Systemic corticosteroid effects with high/prolonged exposure
redFlags: Severe acute dyspnea not responding to rescue plan
teaching: Use exactly as prescribed, rinse and spit after use, and know which inhaler is for rapid relief.
delegationScope: PNs may administer/reinforce technique; assessment of uncontrolled asthma or escalating respiratory distress requires RN/provider escalation.
examTrap: Assuming every inhaler containing formoterol is automatically the patient’s emergency rescue drug.
oneLinePearl: Combination inhalers only work safely when the patient knows their exact role.

title: Roflumilast: COPD Exacerbation Prevention, Not Bronchodilation
bottomLine: Oral roflumilast is a PDE-4 inhibitor used to reduce exacerbation risk in selected severe COPD with chronic bronchitis; it is not a bronchodilator and does not relieve acute bronchospasm.
recognize: Weight loss, diarrhea, nausea, insomnia, anxiety, depression, and suicidality can occur.
Clinical benefit is preventive rather than immediately perceptible bronchodilation.
priorities: Screen for important psychiatric history and baseline weight.
Escalate new suicidal thinking or marked unexplained weight loss.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, mood/behavior, sleep, GI tolerance, COPD exacerbation pattern, and interacting strong CYP inducers.
interventions: Reinforce continuation of prescribed inhaled maintenance and rescue therapies.
medicationSafety: Not for acute bronchospasm.
Avoid strong CYP450 inducers that may reduce exposure; use caution with significant hepatic impairment.
teaching: Report mood changes promptly and track weight if instructed.
Do not use roflumilast instead of rescue medication during acute dyspnea.
delegationScope: PNs may monitor weight/mood and reinforce therapy; suicidality or acute respiratory deterioration requires immediate escalation.
examTrap: Expecting roflumilast to terminate an acute COPD bronchospasm episode.
oneLinePearl: Roflumilast prevents exacerbations; it does not open airways on demand.

title: Omalizumab: Anti-IgE Therapy and Anaphylaxis Readiness
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Omalizumab is anti-IgE biologic therapy used for selected allergic conditions including asthma. Anaphylaxis can occur after administration, so recognition and emergency-response readiness are central nursing safety priorities.
recognize: Bronchospasm, hypotension, syncope, urticaria, throat/tongue swelling, or angioedema after dosing can represent anaphylaxis.
It is maintenance therapy, not acute bronchodilator treatment.
priorities: Verify indication, prescribed dose schedule, allergy history, and emergency-response resources.
Treat suspected anaphylaxis as an emergency rather than as a routine injection reaction.
assessMonitor: Monitor after administration according to current product/facility protocol and assess for delayed hypersensitivity symptoms.
interventions: Administer only where authorized and ensure patient understands delayed anaphylaxis can occur.
medicationSafety: Current labeling carries a boxed warning for anaphylaxis.
Do not substitute for acute asthma rescue treatment.
teaching: Seek emergency care for breathing difficulty, swelling, faintness, or widespread hives after injection.
delegationScope: Biologic administration authority varies; PN monitoring and emergency recognition must follow state/facility policy.
examTrap: Assuming anaphylaxis risk exists only with the first injection.
oneLinePearl: With omalizumab, every dose requires anaphylaxis awareness.

title: Mepolizumab: Eosinophilic Disease Maintenance and Helminth Safety
bottomLine: Mepolizumab is an IL-5 antagonist used as add-on maintenance treatment for eosinophilic disease, including severe eosinophilic asthma and selected COPD patients. It does not treat acute bronchospasm.
recognize: Hypersensitivity may occur after administration.
Pre-existing helminth infection should be treated before therapy when identified.
priorities: Verify phenotype/indication and screen for active infection or hypersensitivity concerns.
Escalate acute asthma/COPD deterioration rather than expecting the biologic to provide immediate rescue.
assessMonitor: Monitor disease control, hypersensitivity, injection-site reactions, and helminth infection concerns.
interventions: Administer per product/facility protocol and reinforce continuation of prescribed controller/rescue regimen.
medicationSafety: Not for acute bronchospasm or status asthmaticus.
Treat pre-existing helminth infection before therapy when possible.
teaching: Keep rescue medication available and report new allergic symptoms or parasitic-infection concerns.
delegationScope: Administration authority varies; PN role centers safe implementation, monitoring, and escalation.
examTrap: Using mepolizumab as the emergency medication during status asthmaticus.
oneLinePearl: Mepolizumab modifies eosinophilic disease over time; it does not rescue acute airflow obstruction.

title: Benralizumab: Eosinophil Depletion and Maintenance Therapy
bottomLine: Benralizumab targets the IL-5 receptor and is used as add-on maintenance therapy for eosinophilic disease. Its role is long-term control, not treatment of acute bronchospasm.
recognize: Headache and pharyngitis are common; hypersensitivity reactions can occur.
Abruptly stopping corticosteroids when biologic therapy begins can cause harm.
priorities: Verify indication and concurrent steroid/controller plan.
Escalate acute respiratory deterioration or hypersensitivity immediately.
assessMonitor: Monitor exacerbation frequency, hypersensitivity, injection reactions, and steroid-withdrawal issues if therapy is being adjusted by the prescriber.
interventions: Administer per product instructions and reinforce that corticosteroid tapering must be prescriber-directed.
medicationSafety: Not for acute bronchospasm.
Do not abruptly discontinue systemic or inhaled corticosteroids solely because benralizumab has started.
complications: Poor disease control if controller regimen is inappropriately reduced
redFlags: Adrenal-insufficiency symptoms after inappropriate steroid withdrawal
teaching: Continue other asthma medicines unless the prescriber changes them.
delegationScope: Biologic administration authority varies; monitoring and escalation are core PN functions.
examTrap: Stopping prednisone immediately once benralizumab is initiated.
oneLinePearl: Biologic control does not justify abrupt steroid withdrawal.

title: Tezepelumab: TSLP Blockade and Severe-Asthma Maintenance
bottomLine: Tezepelumab is a TSLP-blocking biologic used as add-on maintenance therapy for severe asthma and selected chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. It is not indicated for acute bronchospasm or status asthmaticus.
recognize: Hypersensitivity can occur after dosing.
The biologic does not replace acute rescue therapy or automatically eliminate other controllers.
priorities: Verify indication and ongoing controller/rescue plan.
Escalate acute dyspnea and systemic allergic reactions immediately.
assessMonitor: Monitor symptom control, exacerbations, injection reactions, and hypersensitivity.
interventions: Administer per current product instructions and reinforce adherence to the broader respiratory plan.
medicationSafety: Not for relief of acute bronchospasm or status asthmaticus.
Avoid unsupervised abrupt corticosteroid reduction.
teaching: Know which medicine provides quick relief and which medicines prevent future symptoms.
delegationScope: Administration authority varies; acute assessment/escalation remains collaborative.
examTrap: Treating tezepelumab as a rapid-acting bronchodilator.
oneLinePearl: Tezepelumab is maintenance biologic therapy, not rescue therapy.

title: Umeclidinium/Vilanterol: LAMA/LABA COPD Maintenance
bottomLine: Umeclidinium/vilanterol combines a long-acting muscarinic antagonist with a long-acting beta2 agonist for COPD maintenance. It is not a rescue inhaler and is not a substitute for asthma anti-inflammatory therapy.
recognize: Anticholinergic effects include dry mouth, urinary retention, and glaucoma symptoms.
LABA effects can include tremor, palpitations, tachycardia, and hypokalemia.
priorities: Confirm diagnosis/indication and ensure a rescue plan exists.
Review duplicate long-acting bronchodilator therapy.
assessMonitor: Monitor respiratory control, heart rate, urinary symptoms, eye symptoms, and inhaler technique.
interventions: Reinforce once-daily maintenance use as prescribed and correct inhaler activation.
medicationSafety: Not for acute bronchospasm.
Avoid duplicate LABA/LAMA exposure without prescriber review.
teaching: Do not take extra doses for sudden shortness of breath; use the prescribed rescue plan.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and reinforce technique; unstable respiratory symptoms require escalation.
examTrap: Using a LAMA/LABA maintenance inhaler repeatedly during an acute COPD attack.
oneLinePearl: Long-acting bronchodilators maintain airflow; rescue therapy treats sudden obstruction.

title: Nebulized Budesonide in Children: Controller Therapy, Not Rescue
bottomLine: Nebulized budesonide is inhaled corticosteroid maintenance therapy for young children with asthma. It reduces airway inflammation over time and is not the medication for immediate relief of acute bronchospasm.
recognize: Oral candidiasis, dysphonia, and growth effects are corticosteroid-related concerns.
Sudden severe wheeze still requires the child’s rescue/emergency plan.
priorities: Verify nebulizer setup, dose formulation, and that caregiver understands controller-versus-rescue roles.
Assess oral hygiene and growth monitoring plan.
assessMonitor: Monitor symptom control, oral cavity, growth trend, adherence, and frequency of rescue therapy.
interventions: Administer via compatible nebulizer as directed; rinse mouth/clean face after treatment when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Not for acute bronchospasm.
Use the lowest effective corticosteroid exposure consistent with prescribed control plan.
complications: Adrenal suppression with excessive systemic exposure
teaching: This medicine prevents inflammation; the rescue medicine treats sudden tight breathing.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and reinforce caregiver technique; pediatric deterioration requires rapid RN/provider escalation.
examTrap: Waiting for nebulized budesonide to reverse severe acute bronchospasm.
oneLinePearl: Budesonide controls inflammation; it does not replace rescue bronchodilation.
sourceBasis: DailyMed budesonide inhalation suspension labeling updated 2026-02

title: Nebulized Formoterol: Long-Acting COPD Bronchodilation
bottomLine: Nebulized formoterol is a long-acting beta2 agonist for maintenance treatment of COPD bronchoconstriction. It is not a substitute for rapid rescue medication during acute bronchospasm.
recognize: Tremor, tachycardia, palpitations, hypokalemia, or hyperglycemia can occur.
Paradoxical bronchospasm immediately after treatment is an emergency cue.
priorities: Verify COPD maintenance indication and assess for duplicate LABA therapy.
Ensure the patient has the correct acute-rescue plan.
assessMonitor: Monitor respiratory response, heart rate/rhythm, tremor, and signs of paradoxical bronchospasm.
interventions: Administer using the specified nebulizer system and prescribed schedule.
medicationSafety: Maintenance only, not acute rescue.
Avoid additional long-acting beta2 agonists unless specifically ordered.
teaching: Do not increase maintenance LABA dosing for sudden symptoms; follow the rescue plan.
delegationScope: PNs may administer and monitor per policy; acute cardiopulmonary deterioration requires escalation.
examTrap: Giving repeated formoterol nebulizer treatments as if it were a short-acting rescue agent.
oneLinePearl: Formoterol lasts long; that does not make it a rescue drug.
sourceBasis: DailyMed formoterol fumarate inhalation solution labeling updated 2026-03
